<h2 class="accordion-header" id="headingFis">
<button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#collapseFis" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="collapseFis">
<strong>⚛️ Physics and Chemistry</strong>
</button>
</h2>
<div id="collapseFis" class="accordion-collapse collapse" aria-labelledby="headingFis" data-bs-parent="#competenciasAccordion">
<div class="accordion-body">

[**Physics and Chemistry**](https://xtec.gencat.cat/web/.content/curriculum/eso/curriculum-175-2022/Fisica-i-Quimica.pdf){target="_blank"}


Among the aims of the subjects of Physics and Chemistry in compulsory secondary education is the awareness, on the part of students, of the contribution of these sciences to the improvement of the quality of life and to sustainable development, as well as that of awakening curiosity, developing a critical attitude, thinking and scientific skills, the assessment of the role of science, equal opportunities between genders and fostering scientific vocations, especially among male and female students.

Physics and Chemistry from the first to the third year of compulsory secondary education is a subject that all students must take and that establishes some of the minimum bases for scientific literacy and full participation in society. In the fourth year of compulsory secondary education, Physics and Chemistry are optional and their curriculum corresponds to an extension of the subject from first to third. Both subjects contribute to meeting various objectives of compulsory secondary education and to the development of the eight key skills.

In the subjects of Physics and Chemistry, a total of six specific skills are worked on that are the concretization of the descriptors defined in the students' skill profile at the end of basic education. These specific skills can be summarized in: interpretation and prediction of phenomena through physics and chemistry, research in the school environment, generation and interpretation of scientific data, search and management of information, preservation of health and sustainability and the construction of scientific knowledge.

From the subjects of Physics and Chemistry, science is presented as a collective and interdisciplinary process and in continuous construction, which plays a very relevant role in the progress of society. In this sense, the approach to these subjects gives prominence to boys and girls in the work through methodologies specific to science to develop cognitive processes associated with scientific thinking.

In science classrooms, students formulate questions and seek answers based on the problems raised, based on direct or indirect observation of the world in common situations and contexts, the search for evidence and critical inquiry and interpretation, based on scientific knowledge, of information from various sources.

The approach to scientific subjects must encourage students to be aware of the common aspects between biology, geology, physics and chemistry. Scientific subjects share methodologies and ways of working that are transversal, such as identifying regularities in different phenomena, relating causes and effects and investigating changes, among others.

The subject of physics and chemistry contributes to improving skills in information management, given that some specific skills are related to interpreting scientific data and selecting, contrasting, organizing and critically evaluating information. The subject also contributes to the application of various knowledge, such as in the case of research, problem solving or the interpretation of natural phenomena and processes of everyday life related to physics and chemistry.

All these learnings must be applied to real and problematic current contexts and situations, they must allow them to review and evaluate ideas, thoughts or reasoning, making justified proposals for action that are consistent with the arguments stated and grounded in physics and chemistry. In this sense, the sustainable development goals provide these situations, especially in the following cases:

SDG 6. Clean water and sanitation. Guarantee the availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation conditions.

ODS 7. Clean and affordable energy. Guarantee everyone's access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and renewable energy sources.

SDG9. Innovation and [infrastructures](https://ca.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructures){target="_blank"}. Build resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialization and foster innovation.

ODS 11. Sustainable cities and communities. Making cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable.

ODS 12. Responsible consumption and production. Guarantee sustainable consumption and production methods.

SDG13. climate action Adopt urgent measures to combat climate change and its effects.

Among other contributions, the Physics and Chemistry subjects of compulsory secondary education help to reason about the phenomena of the natural and techno-scientific environment that contribute to improving the quality of life and the preservation of the environment, with citizen commitment to the common good through the objectives of sustainable development, adopting attitudes such as responsible consumption, environmental care, sustainable scientific-technological development and respect for other living beings.

The teaching-learning of these subjects also helps to consolidate study habits, foster tolerance, solidarity and cooperation, improve skills and promote language improvement, as collaboration and communication are an essential part of scientific work methodologies. From these subjects, it is promoted that this communication and collaboration takes place using different formats and channels, in particular the virtual remote work spaces. It also promotes equal treatment and rejection of discriminatory attitudes based on gender or other factors.

In the same way, the scientific nature of these subjects contributes to awakening in students a creative and entrepreneurial attitude, which is the very essence of all sciences. Research is therefore promoted through observation, experimentation and the search for evidence, as well as the consultation of different sources to solve questions or contrast hypotheses individually and collaboratively.

The main reliable sources of information are accessible via the Internet, where they coexist with biased, incomplete or false information. For this reason, responsible and critical use of information and communication technologies is also encouraged in these subjects.

The skills must be worked on in the context of learning situations connected to reality and which invite students to reflection, collaboration and action.

The achievement of the **specific competences** constitutes the basis for the competence assessment of the students and will be assessed through the assessment criteria. There is no univocal and direct link between evaluation criteria and knowledge; specific skills will be assessed through the implementation of different knowledge, providing the necessary flexibility to establish connections between them.

Approaching a competence approach, the **evaluation criteria and knowledge**, graduated through the cycles, are structured around specific competences. This progression, which starts from very close and manipulative environments connecting with the stages of infant and primary education, facilitates the transition towards more formal learning and favors the development of the ability to think abstractly.

The assessment criteria, as they explain the assessment of the skills and knowledge that needs to be developed, specify the learning we want to identify in the students and the way to do it. They are directly linked to specific skills. The assessment criteria make it possible to measure the degree of development of these skills and the teacher can flexibly connect them with the knowledge of the area/subject during the teaching-learning process.

The teaching staff must contextualize and make these criteria more flexible in accordance with the circumstances of their activity. Their character is markedly competitive and makes them evaluators of both the capabilities deployed and the different types of knowledge, that is, knowledge, skills, values ​​and attitudes that students must acquire in order to develop in multiple situations typical of modern society.

With regard to the knowledge of Physics and Chemistry from first to third of compulsory secondary education, there is continuity with some learning in the area of ​​Knowledge of the Natural, Social and Cultural Environment of primary education.

Next, the blocks of knowledge that will be worked on throughout compulsory secondary education are described.

The knowledge of this subject includes knowledge, skills and basic attitudes of these areas of knowledge and are structured in what have traditionally been the large knowledge blocks of physics and chemistry: matter, energy, interaction and change. In addition, this curriculum proposes the existence of a block, *basic scientific skills,* of common knowledge that refers to the methodologies of science and their importance in the development of these areas of knowledge. This blog also establishes the relationship between science and one of its most powerful tools, mathematics, which offers a formal language of communication and which includes the students' prior knowledge and those acquired throughout this educational stage.

In the *matter* block, students work on basic knowledge about the constitution of matter formed by chemical elements, relating the properties of elementary and compound substances, on a macroscopic and submicroscopic scale, with varying degrees of depth to connect them with later courses.

In the *energy* blog, students deepen the knowledge they acquired in primary education, such as sources of energy and their practical uses, or the basic concepts about forms of energy. It also acquires at this stage the skills and attitudes that are related to the social and economic development of the real world and its environmental implications.

The *interaction* block describes the main effects of the fundamental interactions of nature and the basic study of the main forces of the natural world, as well as their practical applications in fields such as kinematics, astronomy, sport, engineering, architecture or design.

Finally, the *changes* blog addresses the main physical and chemical transformations of material and natural systems, as well as the most frequent examples of the environment and its applications and contributions to the creation of a better world.

All these curricular elements, specific skills, evaluation criteria and basic knowledge are related to each other, forming a whole that gives the curriculum of this subject an integral and holistic meaning, a relationship to which any classroom program should also aspire.

The construction of science and the development of scientific thinking in adolescence starts from the approach of scientific questions based on the direct or indirect observation of the world in usual situations and contexts, in its attempt to explain based on knowledge, the search for evidence and inquiry and in the correct interpretation of the information that reaches the public daily in different formats from different sources. For this reason, the approach to the subjects of physics and chemistry throughout this educational stage must include an experimental and practical treatment in relation to conceptual knowledge, which expands the students' experience and allows connections to be made with everyday situations, a fact that will contribute significantly to making everyone develop the skills characteristic of science. In this way, it is intended to promote the creation of scientific vocations in students in order to achieve a greater number of students who choose to continue their training in scientific itineraries in the later educational stages and in turn provide a complete scientific basis for those students who wish to study non-scientific itineraries.

The knowledge mentioned above is acquired linked to the development of subject-specific skills which is the true purpose, because these contribute to the improvement of key skills. In other words, the knowledge is part of the specific skills, and their learning is linked to the development of skills, knowledge and skills, and they cannot be worked on in an exclusive way.

The evaluation criteria make it possible to measure the degree of development of the skills and the teacher can connect them flexibly with the knowledge of the subject during the teaching-learning process. Competences and knowledge must be worked on in the form of learning situations or activities with a clear objective, connected to reality and inviting students to reflect and collaborate. For this purpose, interdisciplinary work is recommended, which promotes a deeper understanding of this subject, and connects to other branches of knowledge with which it is linked. In conclusion, Physics and Chemistry from first to third and fourth years of compulsory secondary education work on knowledge of the fundamental experimental sciences as a way to develop basic skills and aim as the ultimate goal of full civic integration of students in the professional, social and emotional sphere.

In Physics and Chemistry, a total of 6 specific skills are worked on, which are the concretization of the operational indicators of the key skills defined in the students' exit skill profile at the end of basic education.

## Specific competence 1

**Interpret natural phenomena, predicting and arguing their behavior based on models, laws and theories specific to physics and chemistry to appropriate concepts and processes specific to science.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 1.1 Analyze concepts, phenomena and processes related to the knowledge of physics and chemistry by interpreting information in different formats (models, graphs, tables, diagrams, formulas, schemes, symbols, web pages...), maintaining a critical attitude and obtaining conclusions based on scientific reasons.  1.2 Interpret and predict the behavior of relevant everyday phenomena, relating it to appropriate models, laws and theories of physics and chemistry.  1.3 Identify concepts related to real problem situations of a scientific nature and provide possible solutions. | 1.1 Analyze concepts, phenomena and processes related to the knowledge of physics and chemistry by interpreting information in different formats (models, graphs, tables, diagrams, formulas, diagrams, symbols, web pages...), maintaining a critical attitude and obtaining conclusions based on scientific reasons and judiciously defending one's own well-founded opinions.  1.2 Interpret and predict the behavior of everyday phenomena, arguing it rigorously in accordance with appropriate models, laws and theories of physics and chemistry.  1.3 Identify the concepts related to real problematic situations of a scientific nature, provide possible solutions and argue their validity. |

The essence of scientific thinking is to find out what are the reasons for the phenomena that occur in the natural environment in order to try to explain them through suitable scientific, physical and chemical models. The interpretation of phenomena involves the argumentation of the causes that originate them and their nature, and gives the student the ability to act with a critical sense to improve, as far as possible, the nearby reality through science.

Physics and chemistry are empirical disciplines that often use logical reasoning and mathematical methodology to create models, solve questions and problems, and validate the results or solutions obtained.

The development of this specific competence entails asking questions to understand what the nature of the environment is like, what are the interactions that occur between the different material systems and what are the causes and consequences of these. This understanding provides critical foundations for decision-making, activates problem-solving processes and in turn enables the creation of new scientific knowledge through the interpretation of phenomena, the use of scientific tools and the analysis of the results obtained. All these processes are related to the rest of the specific skills and are included in the development of scientific thinking, a particularly important issue in the comprehensive training of competent students.

## Specific competence 2

**Design, develop and communicate the research approach and conclusions, including the formulation of questions and hypotheses and their experimental comparison, within the school environment, following the steps of the methodologies of science, such as experimentation and the search for evidence, and computational thinking cooperating, when necessary, to investigate aspects related to physics and chemistry.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 2.1 Ask questions about everyday phenomena and formulate hypotheses that can be answered or contrasted in the school context through experimentation, data collection and analysis of physical and chemical phenomena.  2.2 Design, using methodologies specific to science, research procedures that involve the use of deduction, experimental work and logical-mathematical reasoning.  2.3 Carry out experimental designs using the appropriate instruments, tools or techniques correctly and interpret the results using, when necessary, mathematical and technological tools.  2.4 Cooperate in a scientific project by responsibly assuming a specific function, using virtual spaces when necessary, respecting diversity and promoting inclusion.  2.5 Present the results and conclusions obtained through experimentation and field observation using the appropriate format (tables, graphs, reports, etc.) and, when necessary, digital tools.  2.6 Value the contribution of science to society and the work of the people who have dedicated themselves to it, reflecting on gender bias in science and technology, and understanding research as a collective and interdisciplinary task in constant evolution, influenced by the political context and economic resources. | 2.1 Ask questions about everyday phenomena and formulate hypotheses that can be answered or contrasted in the school context through experimentation, data collection and analysis of physical and chemical phenomena, differentiating them from those pseudoscientific questions that do not admit of experimental verification.  2.2 Design, using methodologies specific to science, research procedures that involve the use of deduction, experimental work and logical-mathematical reasoning.  2.3 Carry out the proposed experiment using the appropriate instruments, tools or techniques with correctness and interpret the results, when necessary, with mathematical and technological tools to obtain reasoned and grounded conclusions or assess the impossibility of doing so.  2.4 Establish collaborations when necessary in the different phases of the scientific project to work more efficiently, valuing the importance of cooperation in research, respecting diversity and promoting inclusion.  2.5 Present clearly and rigorously the results and conclusions obtained through experimentation, arguing the connection between them, and field observation using the appropriate format (tables, graphs, reports, etc.) and digital tools.  2.6 Value the contribution of science to society and the work of the people who have dedicated themselves to it, arguing about gender bias in science and technology and understanding research as a collective and interdisciplinary task in constant evolution, influenced by the political context and economic resources. |

An inherent characteristic of science and the development of scientific thinking in adolescence is the curiosity to know, describe and interpret natural phenomena. Equipping students with scientific skills involves working with the methodologies of science and recognizing and valuing its importance in society. Students who develop this competence must observe, formulate hypotheses and apply experimentation, inquiry and the search for evidence to verify it and predict possible changes.

Using the specific knowledge that students acquire as they progress in their basic training and having a complete collection of scientific resources, such as laboratory techniques or information treatment and selection techniques, are fundamental support for the development of this competence. Students who develop this competence use the mechanisms of scientific thinking to interact with everyday reality and have the ability to rationally and critically analyze the information that comes from observations of their environment, or that they receive through any other means, and express and argue it in scientific terms.

## Specific competence 3

**Generate, interpret and validate data and information in different formats and sources, using appropriately the specific scientific language of physics and chemistry, and use laboratory material responsibly and safely, to value scientific language as a universal tool for communication and knowledge exchange.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 3.1 Generate and use data from various sources and formats (texts, tables, graphics, diagrams, etc.) to interpret, validate and communicate information related to a specific physical or chemical process, through the critical selection of what is most relevant to solving the problem.  3.2 Use appropriately the basic rules of physics and chemistry, including the use of measurement units, mathematical tools and IUPAC formulation and nomenclature, as basic elements of scientific language and effective communication for the exchange of knowledge among the scientific community.  3.3 Use in a practical and responsible manner the rules for the use of specific science spaces, such as the physics and chemistry laboratory, as a means of preserving personal and collective health, the sustainable conservation of the environment and respect for the facilities. | 3.1 Generate and use data from various sources and formats (texts, tables, graphics, diagrams, etc.) to interpret, validate and communicate information related to a specific physical or chemical process, through the critical selection of what is most relevant to solving the problem.  3.2 Use appropriately the basic rules of physics and chemistry, including the appropriate use of various systems of measurement units, the necessary mathematical tools and IUPAC formulation and nomenclature, as basic elements of scientific language and effective communication for the exchange of knowledge among the scientific community.  3.3 Use in a practical, responsible and rigorous manner the rules for the use of specific science spaces, such as the physics and chemistry laboratory, as a means of ensuring personal and collective health, the sustainable conservation of the environment and respect for the facilities. |

The correct interpretation and communication of information play a very important role in the construction of scientific thinking, as they give students the ability to communicate in the universal language of science, beyond the geographical and cultural borders of the world. With the development of this competence, it is intended that students become familiar with the multidirectional information flows characteristic of scientific disciplines and with the rules that the entire scientific community recognizes as universal to establish effective communications included in an environment that ensures health and sustainable environmental development. In addition, it requires students to evaluate the quality of the data and value its imprecision, as well as to recognize the importance of research prior to a scientific study.

With this specific competence, we want to promote the acquisition of knowledge, skills and attitudes related to the multidisciplinary nature of science, the application of rules, the interrelation of variables, the ability to argue, the assessment of the importance of using a universal language, the assessment of diversity, respect for established rules and agreements, for oneself, for others and for the environment, etc., which are fundamental in the scientific fields to be part of a social and community environment wider

## Specific competence 4

**Critically and efficiently use technological platforms and varied resources, both for individual and team work, for the search for information, the creation of materials and communication based on knowledge of physics and chemistry, environmental phenomena and eco-socially relevant issues.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 4.1 Critically, creatively and efficiently use digital environments and different resources in various formats to defend one's point of view on eco-socially relevant phenomena and issues.  4.2 Justify your own point of view on eco-socially relevant issues, using both individual and team work, respecting everyone's contributions and promoting gender and social inclusion.  4.3 Search and analyze information with conventional and digital media and create content related to physics and chemistry, judiciously selecting the most reliable sources and organizing information through the correct use and citation of different sources. | 4.1 Critically, creatively and efficiently use digital environments and different resources in various formats to defend one's point of view on eco-socially relevant phenomena and issues.  4.2 Justify your own point of view on eco-socially relevant issues, using both individual and team work, respecting everyone's contributions and promoting gender and social inclusion.  4.3 Search and analyze information with conventional and digital media and create content related to physics and chemistry, judiciously selecting the most reliable sources and organizing information through the correct use and citation of sources, with respect for intellectual property. |

Resources, both traditional and digital, play a crucial role in the teaching and learning process in general, and in the achievement of skills in particular, since a well-selected resource facilitates the development of higher-level cognitive processes and fosters understanding, creativity and the personal and group development of students. The importance of resources, not only used for the search, analysis, communication and argumentation of information, but also for other purposes such as the creation of teaching materials or effective communication with other members of their learning environment, provides students with the tools to adapt to a society that currently demands people who are integrated and committed to their environment.

It is for this reason that this specific competence also aims for the student to make appropriate use of resources and varied collaboration and cooperation techniques, to analyze their environment and locate certain needs that allow them to devise, design and manufacture products that offer value to themselves and others.

## Specific competence 5

**Analyze the effects of certain actions on the environment and health, based on the foundations of the physical and chemical sciences, to make proposals for action to decide in an informed manner on current problems and adopt habits that minimize environmental impacts, that are compatible with sustainable development and that allow maintaining and improving individual and collective health.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 5.1 Justify with scientific foundations the importance of preserving the physicochemical systems of the environment (air, water, soil quality).  5.2 Justify the need to have sustainable habits, critically analyzing one's own and others' activities and based on one's own reasoning, acquired knowledge and available information.  5.3 Identify some situations in which knowledge derived from physics and chemistry can contribute to improving environmental sustainability and individual and collective health.  5.4 Undertake, in a guided manner and with the appropriate methodology, scientific projects related to the improvement of society and that promote growth among peers as the basis of a critical and ethical school scientific community. | 5.1 Justify with scientific foundations the importance of air quality, of the balance in its composition at the various atmospheric levels, of water currents and soil free of pollutants and sustainable development and identify the possible natural risks enhanced by certain human actions on the physical-chemical systems of the environment 5.2 Argue about the need to have sustainable habits, analyzing own and other people's actions (consumption habits, waste generation, transport, etc.), with a critical attitude and based on the fundamentals of the functioning of natural systems.  5.3 Argue, justifying the reasons provided, about how the knowledge derived from physics and chemistry can contribute to improving environmental sustainability and individual and collective health.  5.4 Undertake, autonomously with the appropriate methodology, scientific projects related to the improvement of society and that promote growth among peers as the basis of a critical and ethical school scientific community. |

The scientific disciplines are characterized by forming a whole of integrated and interrelated knowledge. In the same way, people dedicated to science develop teamwork skills, since collaboration and cooperation are the basis of the construction of scientific knowledge in every society. Competent students will be accustomed to the working methods of the most common techniques of all scientific disciplines, due to the fact that this is the way to achieve, through entrepreneurship, integration into an evolving society. Teamwork serves to unite different points of view and create unified research models, which are part of the progress of science.

The development of this specific competence creates a bond of commitment between the students and their team, as well as with the environment that surrounds them, which enables them to understand what are the most important situations and problems in today's society and how to improve it, how to act to improve their own and community health and what are the habits of life that allow them to act in a sustainable way for the conservation of the environment from a scientific and technological point of view.

## Specific competence 6

**Interpret and value science as a collective construction in continuous change and evolution, which requires interaction with the rest of society to generate improvements that have an impact on technological, economic, environmental and social progress.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 6.1 Interpret science as a process under construction, through the analysis with a historical perspective of the scientific advances of the men and women who participated in it, and value the mutual repercussions of current science with technology, society and the environment.  6.2 Reason the capacity of science to propose, through citizen involvement, sustainable solutions for technological, environmental, economic and social needs, detected in the environment, without gender bias. | 6.1 Interpret science as a process under construction, both through the analysis with a historical perspective of the scientific advances of the men and women who participated in it, as well as current lines of research, and assess the mutual repercussions and the social, economic and environmental implications of current science in society.  6.2 Argue the capacity of science to propose, through citizen involvement, sustainable solutions for technological, environmental, economic and social needs, detected in the environment, without gender bias. |

To complete the development of competence in the subject of Physics and Chemistry, the student must assume that science is not a finished process, but is in a continuous reciprocal construction with technology and society. The search for new explanations, the improvement of procedures, new scientific discoveries, etc. they influence society, and knowing the impacts that science produces in a global way is fundamental in choosing the right path for development. Along these lines, competent students must take into account values ​​such as the importance of scientific advances for a demanding society, the limits of science, ethical issues and trust in scientists and their activity.

All of this is part of a social awareness in which not only the scientific community intervenes, but which requires the participation of all of society, as it implies joint individual and social progress.

### Knowledge

Knowledge is formulated in relation to contexts in which competence learning can be developed. Teachers can incorporate alternative contexts if they consider it relevant.

In order to facilitate learning and the development of the corresponding specific skills, teachers can assess the possibility of organizing the knowledge of the subject, or of the different subjects coordinated in an area, based on situations.

The situations make it possible to program the course of any level, subject or area from a collection or sequence of challenges, contexts, circumstances of the real world, from which derive questions that need to be answered and that intertwine knowledge, that is, knowledge, skills, values ​​and attitudes with the capacities that support the competence approach to learning. This modifies the usual planning for the acquisition of knowledge and skills based on the academic logic specific to the areas of knowledge or subjects, embodied in the traditional sequence of disciplinary subjects. It aims to approach the learner's logic to give meaning to their learning based on the sequence of relevant contexts embodied in the situations.

**First, second and third year**

**Basic Science Skills**

- Use of methodologies specific to scientific research for the identification and formulation of questions, the development of hypotheses and their experimental contrast.
- Designing and carrying out experimental work and entrepreneurship of research projects for problem solving by using experimentation, inquiry, deduction, the search for evidence or logical-mathematical reasoning to make valid inferences from observations and the elaboration of relevant and general conclusions that go beyond the experimental conditions, to apply them to new scenarios.
- Use of various scientific learning environments and resources, such as the laboratory or virtual environments, using the materials, products and technological tools correctly and following the rules of use of each space to ensure the preservation of own and community health, network security and respect for the environment.
- Use of scientific language, including the appropriate use of representations, unit systems and mathematical tools, to achieve reasoned communication in different scientific and learning environments.
- Interpretation and production of scientific information in different formats and with different means to develop an own criterion based on what scientific thinking contributes to the improvement of society.
- Valuation of scientific culture and the role of scientists in the main historical and current milestones of physics and chemistry, highlighting invisible female references, for the advancement and improvement of an equitable and plural society.

**The matter**

- Application of the kinetic model of matter and kinetic molecular theory based on observations of matter to explain its properties, states of aggregation and changes of state, and the formation of mixtures and solutions.
- Carrying out experiments related to material systems to learn about and describe their properties, composition and classification.
- Differentiation of substances and mixtures by their properties, and of elementary and compound substances.
- Identification of the criteria for ordering the elements in the periodic table and their usefulness.
- Application of knowledge about the atomic structure of matter to understand the formation of ions, the existence of isotopes and their properties, the historical development of the atomic model and its contribution to the ordering of the elements in the periodic table.
- Relationship between the physical and chemical properties of elementary substances and the situation of the corresponding elements in the periodic table.
- Assessment of the applications of the main chemical compounds, their formation and their physical and chemical properties, as well as the expression of the amount of matter.
- Appropriate use of a common and universal scientific language through the formulation and naming of simple substances, monatomic ions and most common binary compounds using the IUPAC nomenclature rules.

**The Energy**

- Formulation of questions and hypotheses about energy, manifestations and properties for the development of explanations in relation to change processes.
- Reasoning of the energetic aspects associated with physical changes and chemical changes and their identification in everyday phenomena.
- Experimentation with everyday materials of energy transfer phenomena in the form of light and sound.
- Representation and interpretation of temperature graphs, time in heating and cooling processes and state changes.
- Design and experimental verification of hypotheses related to the domestic and industrial use of energy in its various forms and its transfers and transformations.
- Grounded development of hypotheses about the environment and sustainability based on the differences between renewable and non-renewable energy sources and their contrast with real data and reasoned decision-making.
- Analysis and application of the mechanisms and effects of heat transfer and conduction on material systems (fluids and solids), the achievement of thermal equilibrium, in everyday situations of environmental and social relevance.
- Carrying out experiments related to the electrical nature of matter, and checking and interpreting the conductive properties of materials.
- Design, assembly and analysis of elementary electrical circuits, both in a physical and simulated environment.
- Critical analysis of the different processes of obtaining electrical energy, to develop awareness of the need for energy saving and sustainable conservation of the environment and society.

**Interaction**

- Prediction of the fundamental characteristics of the movement of objects based on the concepts of kinematics, to formulate hypotheses about future values ​​of these magnitudes, through the use of elementary numerical calculation, the interpretation of graphics and the design, assembly and analysis of experimental activities as tools for contrasting hypotheses related to the movement of objects.
- Differentiation of the effects of forces, as agents of change both in the state of movement or rest of a body, as well as producers of deformations, with the changes they produce in the systems on which they act.
- Description of the effects of forces based on observations of everyday phenomena or simulated situations in the laboratory.
- Application of Newton's laws to understand how material systems behave under the action of forces and predict their effects in everyday and road safety situations.
- Identification and comparison of the elastic properties of materials and their use.

**The Change**

- Analysis of the different types of changes experienced by material systems to relate them to the causes that produce them and to the consequences they have.
- Differentiation of physical changes and chemical changes based on experimental evidence and the concept of substance.
- Interpretation of chemical reactions on a macroscopic and submicroscopic scale to explain the relationships of chemistry with the environment, technology and society.
- Search for similarities and differences between processes involving acids and bases, oxidations and precipitate formations and interpretation of the properties of the substances involved in everyday and current contexts.
- Application of the law of conservation of mass and the law of defined proportions, to use them as experimental evidence, and interpretation on the basis of the atomic-molecular model of matter.
- Analysis of the factors that affect chemical reactions to predict their evolution in a qualitative way and assessment of the contribution of various areas of chemistry in solving current problems, sustainable development, health and well-being and everyday products.

**Fourth year**

**Basic scientific skills**

- Design of experimental work and entrepreneurship of research projects for problem solving by using experimentation and error handling, inquiry, deduction, search for evidence or logical-mathematical reasoning to make valid inferences on the basis of observations and draw relevant and general conclusions that go beyond the experimental conditions to apply them to new scenarios.
- Use of various scientific learning environments and resources, such as the laboratory or virtual environments, using the materials, substances and technological tools correctly and following the rules of use of each space to ensure the preservation of own and community health, network security and respect for the environment.
- Use of scientific language, including the appropriate use of unit systems and basic mathematical tools, to argue and communicate in different scientific and learning environments.
- Interpretation and production of scientific information in different formats and from different media to develop an own criterion based on the contributions of science to the improvement of society.
- Assessment of scientific culture and the role of scientists in the main historical and current milestones of physics and chemistry for the advancement and improvement of society.

**The Matter**

- Carrying out activities of a varied nature on the most common material systems, including dissolutions and dispersed systems, for the resolution of problems related to various everyday situations.
- Argumentation and prediction of the macroscopic properties of various substances (state, conductivity, density, boiling and melting temperature...) in relation to the type of substance and its structure.
- Recognition of the main atomic models and the constituents of atoms to establish the relationship with the most relevant advances in physics and chemistry in recent history.
- Relation, based on their electronic configuration, of the distribution of the elements in the periodic table with their most important physicochemical properties, to find generalities.
- Assessment of the usefulness of chemical compounds based on their properties in relation to how atoms are combined, as a way of recognizing the importance of the applications of chemistry in different areas.
- Simple calculations using the amount of matter in everyday situations and of special relevance and interest, using scientific language appropriately.
- Appropriate use of the formulation and nomenclature of the most common inorganic chemical compounds using the IUPAC rules.
- Introduction to the formulation and nomenclature of organic compounds using the IUPAC rules, as a basis for understanding the wide variety of carbon-based compounds in the environment.

**The Energy**

- Formulation and verification of hypotheses about the different forms of energy and their applications based on their properties and the principle of conservation, for the resolution of problems related to mechanical energy in everyday situations of social relevance.
- Recognition of the different energy transfer processes in which forces or temperature differences are involved, as a basis for solving everyday problems.
- Estimation of energy values ​​and energy consumption in everyday situations through the application of knowledge, the search for proven information, experimentation and scientific reasoning to debate and understand the importance of energy in society and its responsible use.

**The interaction**

- Prediction and verification, using experimentation and logical-mathematical reasoning, of the main magnitudes, equations and graphs that describe the movement of a body, to relate it to everyday situations and the improvement of the quality of life.
- Recognition of strength as an agent of changes in bodies that is applied to other fields such as design, sport or engineering, among others.
- Use of vector representation in graphics and numerical operations with forces and its application to solving problems related to systems subjected to sets of forces, and assessment of its importance in everyday situations.
- Identification and representation of the main forces in the everyday environment, such as weight, normal, friction, tension or thrust, and their use in explaining physical phenomena in different contexts.
- Assessment of the effects of applied forces in liquids and gases, and especially the concept of pressure, and its effects in different situations.

**The Change**

- Using the information contained in a fitted chemical equation and the most relevant laws of chemical reactions to make qualitative and quantitative predictions by experimental and numerical methods, and relate this to the physicochemical processes of industry, the environment and society.
- Qualitative description of chemical reactions in the everyday environment, including combustions, neutralizations and electrochemical processes, experimentally checking some of the parameters, to make an assessment of their implications for technology, society or the environment.
- Relation of basic thermodynamic and kinetic variables to chemical reactions, applying models such as collision theory, to explain the rearrangement of atoms and make predictions applied to the most important everyday processes.

<div class="accordion-item">
<h2 class="accordion-header" id="headingCultura">
<button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#collapseCultura" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="collapseCultura">
<strong>🔬 Scientific Culture</strong>
</button>
</h2>
<div id="collapseCultura" class="accordion-collapse collapse" aria-labelledby="headingCultura" data-bs-parent="#competenciasAccordion">
<div class="accordion-body">

[**Scientific Culture**](https://xtec.gencat.cat/web/.content/curriculum/eso/curriculum-175-2022/Cultura-Cientifica.pdf "Cultura Científica"){target="_blank"} **(elective subject of fourth year of ESO)**

In the 21st century, science is everywhere, permeates the environment and conditions our lives, being inseparable from all the most relevant economic and social areas. In this sense, scientific literacy becomes essential for the knowledge and understanding of scientific concepts and the processes necessary for making personal and collective decisions. It becomes an indispensable means for effective participation in the societies and economy of the millennium.

Nevertheless, science is inherent in the existence and progress of humanity. For many centuries natural history, philosophy and belief blurred into an incoherent continuum that sought to provide answers to the most vital questions. It was not until the 16th and 17th centuries that the scientific revolution gave way to modern science, which increased its influence on the social, intellectual and economic movement of the time.

Scientific culture, in a broad sense, is present in our society, in the past, present and future. As a way of life, culture primarily refers to the collective concepts, values, behaviors and patterns that are unique and inherited by a society. Science constitutes a multidisciplinary and inclusive space, open to innovative perspectives in the understanding of the world, the development of technology, the promotion of health and the economy. It is not science *per se*, but it gives us a unique perspective, a system of values ​​and a way of thinking that defines fairer and more sustainable societies. Scientific knowledge offers a way of looking at and knowing the world around us, which adds great potential for social transformation. It is this transformation that, with the social and ethical aspects, can allow a critical capacity to improve society and people.

Scientific culture and the activities that enable its understanding, development and application have various impacts and objectives. Individually, their immediate impact consists of increasing curiosity and interest in science and technology, awakening vocations and breaking outdated stereotypes that have persisted over time. Collectively, the understanding and achievement of their knowledge contributes to the improvement of the quality of life and sustainable development, to the promotion of curiosity and critical attitude, to thinking and open-mindedness, to scientific skills and creativity, to the appreciation of the role of science and to equal opportunities.

Scientific culture is, therefore, a form of collective intelligence that allows us to become aware of the common good in the scientific, social, political and technological fields. A population with a great scientific culture will be able to have a critical and analytical view of the society around it.

In the subject of Scientific Culture, a total of four specific skills are worked on, which are the concretization of the descriptors defined in the student's skill profile at the end of basic education. These specific skills can be summarized in: analysis and interpretation of data, understanding of phenomena and adequate communication of the conclusions obtained from the analysis, efficient management of the information available in different formats and platforms for the construction of knowledge, study of the scientific foundations for the preservation of health and sustainability and the construction of fairer and more sustainable coexistence spaces based on scientific knowledge and citizen science.

From the subject of Scientific Culture, science is presented as a collective and interdisciplinary process and in continuous construction, which plays a very relevant role in the progress of society. In this sense, the focus of this subject gives prominence to boys and girls in the work through methodologies specific to science to develop cognitive and metacognitive processes associated with scientific thinking.

The approach to this subject must encourage students to be aware of the common and interrelated aspects between physics, chemistry, biology, geology and technology. Scientific subjects share methodologies and ways of working that are transversal, such as identifying regularities and patterns in different phenomena, relating causes and effects and investigating changes, among others.

The subject of Scientific Culture contributes to improving skills in information management, given that some specific skills are related to interpreting scientific data and selecting, comparing, organizing and critically evaluating information. This subject also contributes to the application of various methodologies and knowledge, such as research, problem solving or the interpretation of natural phenomena and processes of everyday life related to science.

All these learnings must be applied to real and problematic current contexts and situations, they must allow them to review and evaluate ideas, thoughts or reasoning, making proposals for actions or performances that are justified and consistent with the arguments stated and grounded in science. In this sense, the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) provide these situations, especially in the following cases:

- SDG 1. Zero hunger. End hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition and promote sustainable agriculture. More than 800 million people are undernourished.
- SDG 2. Health and well-being. Ensuring healthy living and promoting well-being for all at all ages. More than 5 million children die before the age of five.
- SDG 6. Clean water and sanitation. Guarantee the availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation conditions.
- ODS 7. Clean and affordable energy. Guarantee everyone's access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and renewable energy sources.
- Reduction of inequalities. Reduce inequality in and between countries. It is necessary to pay attention to the needs of the most marginalized and disadvantaged people in order to achieve social sustainability.
- ODS 11. Sustainable cities and communities. Making cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable.
- ODS 12. Responsible consumption and production. Guarantee sustainable consumption and production methods.
- climate action Adopt urgent measures to combat climate change and its effects.
- underwater life Conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources. Marine water pollution endangers many ecosystems and more than 3,000 million people who live from the sea.
- Life of terrestrial ecosystems. Sustainably manage forests, fight desertification, stop and reverse land degradation and halt biodiversity loss.

Among other contributions, the subject of Scientific Culture in the fourth year of ESO contributes to reasoning about the phenomena of the natural and scientific-technological environment that allow, in turn, to improve the quality of life and the preservation of the environment, with citizen commitment for the common good through the objectives of sustainable development, adopting attitudes such as responsible consumption, environmental care, sustainable scientific-technological development and respect for other living beings.

The teaching-learning of this subject also helps to consolidate study habits; promote tolerance, solidarity and cooperation; improve language skills and promote language improvement, since communication is an essential part of scientific work methodologies. From this subject, it is promoted that this communication and collaborative work is done using different formats and channels, in particular virtual spaces for shared work. It also promotes equal treatment and rejection of discriminatory attitudes based on gender or other factors.

In the same way, the scientific nature of this subject contributes to awakening in students a creative and entrepreneurial attitude, which is the very essence of all sciences. Research is therefore promoted through observation, experimentation and the search for evidence, as well as the consultation of different sources to solve questions or contrast hypotheses individually and collaboratively.

The main reliable sources and evidence of information are accessible through the Internet, where they coexist with fake news, biased, incomplete or false information. For this reason, the responsible and critical use of information and communication technologies is also encouraged.

The achievement of the **specific competences** constitutes the basis for the competence assessment of the students and will be assessed through the assessment criteria. There is no univocal and direct link between evaluation criteria and knowledge; specific skills will be assessed through the contextualization of different knowledge, providing the necessary flexibility to establish connections between them.

Approaching a competence approach, the **evaluation criteria** and **knowledge** are structured around specific competences. The progression of the competence approach, which starts from very close and manipulative environments, connecting with the previous stages of education, facilitates the transition towards more formal learning and favors the development of the ability to think abstractly.

The assessment criteria, as they explain the assessment of the skills and knowledge that needs to be developed, specify the learning we want to identify in the students and the way to do it. They are directly linked to specific skills. The evaluation criteria make it possible to measure the degree of achievement of these skills and the teacher can flexibly connect them with the knowledge of the subject during the teaching-learning process.

The teaching staff must contextualize and make these criteria more flexible in accordance with the circumstances of their activity. Their character is markedly competitive and makes them evaluators of both the capabilities deployed and the different types of knowledge, that is, knowledge, skills, values ​​and attitudes that students must acquire in order to develop in multiple situations typical of modern society.

With regard to the knowledge of the subject of Scientific Culture, they are presented as a tour of the most historically relevant scientific topics, but they also contain an important bulk of current topics, which will surely be present throughout the students' lives and which will require them to speak out and act.

The knowledge of this subject includes knowledge, skills and basic attitudes of the knowledge areas of science and are structured in blocks that correspond to the major topics that have traditionally been worked on in the scientific field throughout history: the origin and evolution of the Universe and of life; health science; biotechnology and society, sustainable development, and new materials and technologies.

In the block *the origin and evolution of the Universe and life* students work on the main theories of the formation and evolution of the Universe, relating the formation of matter and chemical elements to the origin of life and the main theories linked to each historical and social context. We leave aside the Cartesian segmentation between the formation of the Earth and life to understand that we are descendants of hominids and bacteria, but also of the stars and galaxies.

In the blog *the science of health* students deepen the knowledge that should allow them to acquire healthier habits and relate to the biomedical context in a solvent and informed way. Topics such as nutrition, diagnostic methods, types of diseases and the appropriate habits to prevent them, but also issues that especially threaten your population group such as eating disorders, addictive substances, pathological dependence on mobile phones and social networks, the risks of self-medication or sexually transmitted diseases.

In the *biotechnology and society* block, the aim is for students to acquire the basic knowledge to understand some applications of biotechnology and its social, ethical and legal implications. This blog is also a clear invitation to make decisions based on science and the rejection of pseudoscience.

In the *sustainable development* blog, some of the most relevant environmental crises are characterized and debated, as well as their economic and social repercussions. Energy and water consumption patterns are analyzed; the convenience, risks and benefits of electric vehicles and autonomous vehicles; renewable energies, and the problem of microplastics, among others. This blog places a special emphasis on the individual contribution in crisis scenarios, to become aware of the importance of the individual and local role in global causes.

Finally, the blog *new materials and technologies* addresses the influence of technological revolutions and their social changes. From here, it prepares the ground to recognize the impact of new materials (nanomaterials and biomaterials) and their fields of application. 5G technology, next-generation mobile sensors, communications between devices, the Internet of Things (IdC) or artificial intelligence are, without a doubt, some of the topics that will have special relevance throughout the students' lives. Finally, this blog will work on the concept of citizen science, which is based on the active participation of citizens in scientific research activities.

All these curricular elements, specific skills, evaluation criteria and basic knowledge, are related to each other forming a whole that gives the curriculum of this subject an integral and holistic meaning, a relationship to which any classroom programming should also aspire.

The construction of science and the development of scientific thinking in adolescence starts from the approach of scientific questions based on the direct or indirect observation of the world in usual situations and contexts, in its attempt to explain based on knowledge, the search for evidence and inquiry and in the correct interpretation of the information that reaches the public daily in different formats from different sources. For this reason, the approach to the subject of Scientific Culture in the fourth year of ESO must include an experimental and practical treatment in relation to conceptual knowledge, which expands the students' experience and allows connections to be made with everyday situations, which will contribute significantly to making everyone develop the characteristic skills of science. In this way, it is intended to promote the creation of scientific vocations in students to achieve a greater number of students who choose to continue their training in scientific itineraries in the later educational stages and provide, in turn, a complete scientific basis for those students who wish to study non-scientific itineraries.

The knowledge mentioned above is acquired linked to the achievement of subject-specific skills, which is the true purpose, because they contribute to the improvement of key skills. In other words, the knowledge is part of the specific skills and their learning is linked to the development of skills and they cannot be worked on in an exclusive way.

The evaluation criteria make it possible to measure the degree of achievement of the skills and the teacher can flexibly connect them with the knowledge of the subject during the teaching-learning process. Competences and knowledge must be worked on in the form of learning situations or activities with a clear objective, connected to reality and inviting students to reflect and collaborate. To this end, interdisciplinary work is recommended, which promotes a deeper understanding of this subject and connects with other branches of knowledge with which it is linked. In conclusion, the subject of Scientific Culture works on knowledge of the fundamental experimental sciences as a way to develop basic skills and aims as the ultimate goal of full civic integration of students in the professional, social and emotional sphere.

In the Scientific Culture subject, a total of 4 specific competences are worked on, which are the realization of the operational indicators of the key competences defined in the exit competence profile of the students at the end of basic education.

**Specific competence 1**

**Analyze and interpret natural phenomena, based on different formats and sources of information****, predicting and arguing their behavior based on models, laws and theories specific to science. Obtain conclusions and communicate them using scientific methodology and language as a knowledge exchange tool.**

**Evaluation criteria**

1.1. Analyze concepts, phenomena and processes related to scientific knowledge by interpreting information in different formats (models, simulators, experimental results, graphs, tables, diagrams, formulas, diagrams, web pages...), maintaining a critical attitude and obtaining conclusions based on scientific reasoning and judiciously defending one's own well-founded opinions.

1.2. Interpret and predict the behavior of everyday phenomena, arguing them with rigor in accordance with appropriate models, laws and theories of science. Communicate predictions and/or conclusions using scientific language and the appropriate supports and formats for each case.

1.3. Identify the concepts related to real problematic situations of a scientific nature, provide possible solutions and present the results and conclusions obtained in a clear and rigorous manner, using the appropriate format and arguing their validity.

The essence of scientific thinking is to find out what are the reasons for the phenomena that occur in the natural environment in order to try to explain them through suitable scientific models. The interpretation of phenomena involves understanding the causes that originate them and their nature, and gives students the ability to act with a critical sense to propose improvements to the reality close to them through science.

The development of this specific competence involves asking questions to understand the nature of the environment, what are the interactions that occur between the different material systems and what are their causes and consequences. This understanding provides critical foundations for decision-making, activates problem-solving processes and, in turn, enables the creation of new scientific knowledge through the interpretation of phenomena, the use of scientific tools and the analysis of the results obtained. All these processes are related to the rest of the specific skills and are included in the development of scientific thinking, a particularly important issue in the comprehensive training of competent students.

The correct interpretation and communication of information play a very important role in the construction of scientific thinking, as they give students the ability to communicate in the universal language of science, beyond the geographical and cultural borders of the world. With the development of this competence, it is intended that students become familiar with the multidirectional information flows characteristic of scientific disciplines and with the rules that the entire scientific community recognizes as universal to establish effective communications included in an environment that ensures health and sustainable environmental development. In addition, it requires students to evaluate the quality of the data and value its imprecision, as well as to recognize the importance of research prior to a scientific study.

With this specific competence we want to promote the acquisition of knowledge, skills and attitudes related to the multidisciplinary nature of science, the application of rules, the interrelationship of variables, the ability to argue, the assessment of the importance of using a universal language, the assessment of diversity, and respect for the established rules and agreements, towards oneself, towards others and towards the environment, which are fundamental in the scientific fields to be part of a more social and community environment wide

**Specific competence 2**

**Critically and efficiently use technological platforms and varied resources,**  **both in individual and team work, for the search for information, the creation of materials and communication based on knowledge of science, surrounding phenomena and socially relevant issues, organizing information through the correct use and citation of sources, with respect for intellectual property.**

**Evaluation criteria**

2.1. Use digital environments and different resources in various formats in a critical, creative and efficient way to present and assertively defend one's point of view on socially relevant phenomena and issues, based on scientific reasoning.

2.2. Construct and justify your own point of view, grounded in science, on socially relevant issues, working both individually and as a team, respecting everyone's contributions and promoting gender and social inclusion.

2.3. Search for and analyze information with conventional and digital media and create content related to science, selecting with judgment the most reliable sources and organizing information through the correct use and citation of sources, with respect for intellectual property.

Resources, both traditional and digital, play a crucial role in the teaching and learning process in general and in the achievement of skills in particular, since a well-selected resource facilitates the development of higher-level cognitive processes and fosters understanding, creativity and the personal and group development of students. The importance of resources, not only used for the search, analysis, communication and argumentation of information, but also for other purposes such as the creation of teaching materials or effective communication with other members of their learning environment, provides students with the tools to adapt to a society that currently demands people who are integrated and committed to their environment.

It is for this reason that this specific competence also aims for the student to make appropriate use of resources and varied collaboration and cooperation techniques, to analyze their environment and locate certain needs that allow them to devise, design and manufacture products that offer value to themselves and others.

**Specific competence 3**

**Analyze the effects of certain actions on the environment and health, based on the foundations of science, to make proposals for actions that allow decisions to be made in an informed and critical manner in current problems, and to recognize and adopt habits that minimize environmental impacts, that are compatible with the objectives of sustainable development (ODS) and that allow maintaining and improving individual and collective health.**

**Evaluation criteria**

3.1. To justify with scientific foundations the importance of air quality, of the balance in its composition at the various atmospheric levels, of water currents and of soil free of pollutants and to identify the possible natural risks enhanced by certain human actions on the physicochemical and biological systems of the environment, for sustainable development.

3.2. Argue about the need to have sustainable habits, analyzing one's own and others' actions (consumption habits, waste generation, transport, etc.), with a critical attitude and based on the fundamentals of the functioning of natural systems.

3.3. Argue, justifying the reasons provided, about how knowledge derived from science can contribute to improving environmental sustainability and individual and collective health.

3.4. Argue about the need to have healthy habits, analyzing one's own and other people's actions (food, hygiene, body posture, physical activity, safe travel, interpersonal relationships, rest, exposure to screens, stress management, safety in sexual practices, substance use, etc.), with a critical attitude and based on the foundations of science.

3.5. Justify with scientific foundations the importance of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in the preservation of biodiversity, the conservation of the environment, the protection of living beings in the environment, sustainable development and the quality of life, and identify the possible natural risks enhanced by certain human actions in a geographical area.

3.6. Undertake, autonomously with the appropriate methodology, scientific projects related to the improvement of society and that promote growth among peers as the basis of a critical and ethical citizen scientific community.

The scientific disciplines are characterized by forming a whole of integrated and interrelated knowledge. In the same way, people dedicated to science develop teamwork skills, since collaboration and cooperation are the basis of the construction of scientific knowledge in every society.

Teamwork serves to unite different points of view and create unified research models, which are the engine of progress in science.

The development of this specific competence creates a bond of commitment between the student and their team, as well as with the environment that surrounds them, which enables them to understand what are the most important situations and problems in today's society and how to improve it, how to act to improve their own and community health and what are the lifestyle habits that allow them to act sustainably for the conservation of the environment from a scientific and technological point of view.

**Specific competence 4**

**Interpret and value science as a collective construction in continuous change and evolution, which requires interaction with the rest of society to generate improvements that have an impact on technological, economic, environmental and social progress, and recognize the value and potential of citizen science as a resource at the service of communities to guarantee access to information, transparency and participation for the construction of fairer and more sustainable societies.**

**Evaluation criteria**

4.1. Interpret science as a process under construction, both through the analysis with a historical perspective of the scientific advances of the men and women who participated in it, as well as current lines of research, and assess the repercussions and the social, economic and environmental implications of current science in society.

4.2. Arguing the capacity of science to propose, through citizen involvement, sustainable solutions for the technological, environmental, economic and social needs detected in the environment, without gender or any other type of bias.

4.3. Identify deficiencies or needs in the immediate environment that can be reduced or solved through actions or simple applications of citizen science that have an impact on promoting the transformation of cities into fairer, kinder and more sustainable habitats. Disseminate or communicate the proposals to the groups indicated when appropriate.

To complete the development of competence in the subject of Scientific Culture, students must assume that science is not a finished process, but is in a continuous reciprocal construction with technology and society. The search for new explanations, the improvement of procedures, new scientific discoveries, etc., influence society and it is essential to know the impact they have on it in order to be able to choose the right path for a more sustainable development. Along these lines, competent students must take into account aspects such as the importance of scientific advances, the limits of science and ethical issues.

All of this is part of a social awareness in which not only the scientific community intervenes, but which requires the participation of all of society, as it implies joint individual and social progress. The identification of upcoming needs or problems invites students to take an active role in building fairer and more sustainable environments.

**Knows**

Knowledge is formulated in relation to contexts in which competence learning can be developed. Teachers can incorporate different contexts if they consider it relevant.

In order to facilitate learning and the achievement of the corresponding specific skills, teachers can assess the possibility of organizing the knowledge of the subject in learning situations.

The learning situations make it possible to program the course of any level or subject from a collection or sequence of challenges, contexts, circumstances of the real world, from which derive questions that need to be answered and that intertwine knowledge, that is, knowledge, skills, values ​​and attitudes, with the capacities that support the competence approach to learning. This modifies the usual planning of acquiring knowledge and achieving skills based on the academic logic specific to the areas of knowledge or subjects, embodied in the traditional sequence of disciplinary subjects. The aim is to arouse the learner's interest in giving meaning to their learning based on the sequence of relevant contexts embodied in the learning situations.

**Origin and evolution of the Universe and of life**

- Theories about the origin of the Universe: from the geocentric to the heliocentric model, from Genesis to the Big Bang. Assessment of changes in paradigms and implications in the social context. Knowledge of instruments and methods for surveying and studying the Universe and matter: from telescopes to particle accelerators. Differentiation between science and pseudoscience in the explanation of the cosmos. Understanding the structure of the Universe: galaxies, stars and planets.
- Contextualization of the Earth within the solar system and the processes of formation and evolution of the stars and chemical elements. Relationship between the chemical elements that make up the Universe, the Earth and our body (the calcium in our bones, the oxygen we breathe, the iron in our blood...), with the life cycle of the stars. How the chemical elements in our cells contain the history of evolution. We are descended from hominids and bacteria, but also from the stars and galaxies.
- Discussion of theories about the origin of life on Earth. Analysis and significance of hominid fossils and knowledge of the main dating methods. Comparison between arguments that support evolutionary ideas: facts, theories and evidence. Necessary conditions for life.

**Health Science**

- The importance of food for health. Consideration of the influence of cultural habits on eating habits. Identification of myths and errors about food and diets. Eating behavior disorders: detection and treatment. Knowledge of the effects on health of the use of some addictive substances.
- The global challenge of food production, global supply and environmental impact. Discussion on the convenience of food sovereignty models against centralized production. Introduction of the concepts of eco-gastronomy (*slow-food*) and local or 0-kilometer products. Food waste.
- Distinction between infectious and non-infectious diseases. Use of antibiotics and bioresistance of bacteria. Increasing antibiotic resistance and consequences for global public health.
- Diseases caused by viruses. Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs). Prevention, importance of early detection and treatment.
- Identification and study of a disease and its social impact: AIDS, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), multiple sclerosis, diabetes, Alzheimer's disease...
- Knowledge and assessment of healthy habits in disease prevention. Main types of medicines and their applications. Risks of self-medication. Understanding of leaflets and labeling.
- Knowledge and classification of diagnostic means (clinical analyses, imaging) and treatments (pharmacology, surgery, chemotherapy, use of radiation and transplants). Assessment of the importance of blood, tissue and organ donation.

**Biotechnology and society**

- Characterization of the basic functional groups of genetics: nucleic acids, gene structure, coding and expression of genetic information. Identification of the genome as a distinctive feature of organisms: relationship between genes and evolution. Critical and ethical evaluation of the contributions and applications of the Human Genome Project.
- Assessment of the social and economic interest of transgenic organisms to face the challenges of the millennium (food production, biofuels, bioplastics...). Risks against Analysis of the forms of human intervention on the genetic diversity of the biosphere and assessment of the associated risks.
- Identification of some applications of biotechnology in medicine and their social, ethical and legal implications. Importance of vaccines as an attitude of individual and collective responsibility. Argument on the controversies related to assisted reproduction, gene therapy and the use of stem cells.

**Sustainable development**

- Characterization and debate of current relevant environmental crises: global warming and climate change, water management, pollution and associated diseases.
