Identification of natural and anthropogenic causes. Differentiation between evidence, theories and possible scenarios. International agreements.
- Economic and social implications of overexploitation of natural resources, deforestation, water scarcity, desertification, loss of biodiversity, impact of microplastics and waste treatment. Associated migratory movements and human, economic and social consequences.
- Introduction to the ODS and assessment of the impact of our habits in such everyday areas as fast fashion (*fast-fashion*), recycling, consumption habits, etc.
- Analysis of energy consumption patterns. Calculation and comparison of energy and water consumption in different societies. Efficiency in the use of fuels for transport. Sustainable mobility, single-person vehicles and electric cars. Energy consumption and saving at home. Assessment of the benefits and limitations of the use of renewable energies. Definition and calculation of the current ecological footprint.
- Characterization of the different conceptions of sustainable development. Relationship between development strategies and social conflicts. Critical assessment of the role of environmental movements and environmental policies at local and international level.

**New materials and technologies**

- Analysis of the influence of technological revolutions, innovations in materials, objects and services, and social changes. Introduction to SWOT analysis (weaknesses, threats, strengths and opportunities) for effective and assertive debate.
- Recognition of the contribution of new materials in the creation of new technological fields: biomaterials and nanomaterials. Characteristics, properties and applications of graphene (nanomaterial) and biomaterials. Problems associated with the exploitation of strategic minerals (for example, coltan).
- Establishing the relationship between materials and resources. Analysis of the impact of consumption habits on the availability of resources based on calculations on the life cycle of various objects and materials. Planned obsolescence. Classification of waste types and their treatment. Evaluation of strategies for saving, reducing, recycling and reusing materials.
- Assessment of the economic, social and cultural implications of information and communication technologies. Knowledge of current telecommunication systems and applications.
- Characterization of the information and knowledge society. Analysis of the impacts of the Internet and the World Wide Web (WWW) on everyday life. Recognition of the ethical dimension and associated risks: the digital divide, privacy and data protection, and cyber culture.
- Characterization, uses and applications of 3D printers, artificial intelligence, 5G technology, next-generation mobile communication sensors, the Internet of Things (IdC) and *makerspaces*.
- Citizen science and its current applications and potential. Visibility and shared data (water and air quality, weather stations...). Definition and design of a smart city project through local initiatives that can have an immediate impact on the community.
</div>
</div>
</div>

<div class="accordion-item">
<h2 class="accordion-header" id="headingMat">
<button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#collapseMat" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="collapseMat">
<strong>📐 Mathematics</strong>
</button>
</h2>
<div id="collapseMat" class="accordion-collapse collapse" aria-labelledby="headingMat" data-bs-parent="#competenciasAccordion">
<div class="accordion-body">

**[Mathematics](https://xtec.gencat.cat/web/.content/curriculum/eso/curriculum-175-2022/Matematiques.pdf "Mathematics"){target="_blank"}**

Mathematics is found in any human activity, from scientific work to cultural and artistic expressions, forming part of the cultural heritage of our society. The mastery of space and time, the organization and optimization of resources, shapes and proportions, the ability to forecast and control uncertainty or the correct use of digital technology are characteristics of mathematics, but also reasoning, argumentation, communication, perseverance, decision-making or creativity. Therefore, it is important to develop in students the aspects of mathematics that allow them to grow and act with knowledge both in personal, academic and scientific as well as social and work contexts.

The curricular development of mathematics is based on the objectives of the stage, paying special attention to the achievement of the key skills established in the students' exit skills profile at the end of basic education. This achievement is an indispensable condition to achieve the personal, social and professional development of students and all subjects must contribute to this achievement, taking as a reference the descriptors established in the Competence Profile. This is also the case with mathematics, which is why they take the output competence profiles as a reference when establishing their own specific competences.

The main lines in the definition of specific mathematics skills are problem solving and socio-emotional skills. In addition, the formulation of conjectures, mathematical reasoning, the establishment of connections between the different mathematical elements, with other subjects and with reality and communication and the different ways of representing mathematical ideas are addressed.

Traditionally, some students have perceived a barrier to learning mathematics. This barrier is largely associated with preconceived ideas about this matter, both at an individual or social level and due to the appearance of negative emotions derived from these unjustified beliefs. Didactic research has shown that performance in mathematics can improve if you help overcome these prejudices and develop positive emotions towards mathematics. Therefore, the mastery of socio-emotional skills such as identifying and managing emotions, facing challenges, maintaining motivation and perseverance and developing self-concept, among others, will allow students to increase their general well-being, build resilience and thrive as a student of mathematics.

On the other hand, solving problems is not only a goal of learning mathematics, but also the way to do it. In solving problems, processes such as the ability to interpret them, the translation into mathematical language, the application of resolution strategies, the evaluation of the process and the verification of the validity of the solution stand out. Related to problem solving is computational thinking, data analysis, the logical organization of this data, the search for solutions in sequences of ordered steps, obtaining solutions with instructions that can be executed by a computer, a person or a combination of both, expand the ability to solve problems and promote the efficient use of technological tools.

The specific competencies are related to each other and have been grouped around five competency blocks according to their nature: *problem solving* (1, 2), *reasoning and proof* (3 and 4), *connections* (5 and 6), *communication and representation* (7) and *social-emotional management* (8 and 9). The mathematics of this stage connects directly with the mathematics of previous stages both in terms of specific skills and assessment criteria as well as knowledge, providing a continuity in the learning of mathematics that respects the psychological development and cognitive progress of students.

The skills must be worked on in the context of learning situations, connected to reality and which invite students to reflect, collaborate and take action.

The achievement of the specific skills constitutes the basis for the student's competence assessment and will be assessed through the assessment criteria. There is no unequivocal and direct link between assessment criteria and knowledge, specific skills are assessed through the implementation of different knowledge, providing the necessary flexibility to establish connections between them.

Approaching a competence approach, the evaluation criteria and knowledge, graduated through the cycles, are structured around specific competences. This progression, which starts from very close and manipulative environments connecting with the stages of infant and primary education, facilitates the transition towards more formal learning and favors the development of the ability to think abstractly.

The assessment criteria, as they explain the assessment of the skills and knowledge that needs to be developed, specify the learning we want to identify in the students and the way to do it. They are directly linked to specific skills. The assessment criteria make it possible to measure the degree of development of these skills and the teacher can flexibly connect them with the knowledge of the subject during the teaching-learning process.

The teaching staff must contextualize and make these criteria more flexible in accordance with the circumstances of their activity. Their character is markedly competitive and makes them evaluators of both the capabilities deployed and the different types of knowledge, that is, knowledge, skills, values ​​and attitudes that students must acquire in order to develop in multiple situations typical of modern society.

The achievement of specific skills is assessed through the evaluation criteria. Accompanying these criteria, a set of knowledge has been drawn up that integrates knowledge, skills and attitudes that will help the achievement of specific skills throughout the stage. Knowledge has been grouped into senses as sets of skills related to the different areas of mathematics: numerical, measurement, algebraic and computational thinking, spatial, stochastic and socio-emotional. These senses allow knowledge to be used in a functional way, providing the necessary flexibility to establish connections between the different senses. It must be taken into account that the organization of knowledge in the curriculum does not imply any timing or chronological order in its treatment in the classroom.

Number sense is characterized by the application of knowledge about numeration and calculation in different contexts, and by the development of skills and ways of thinking based on the understanding, representation and flexible use of numbers and operations.

The sense of measurement focuses on the understanding and comparison of attributes of objects in the natural world. Understanding and choosing the right units to estimate, measure and compare magnitudes, using the right instruments to make measurements, comparing physical objects and understanding the relationships between shapes and measurements are the central axes of this sense.

Spatial sense addresses the understanding of the geometric aspects of our world. Registering and representing shapes and figures, recognizing their properties, identifying their relationships, placing them, describing their movements, creating or discovering images of shapes and figures, classifying them and reasoning about them are fundamental elements of teaching and learning geometry.

The algebraic sense provides the language in which mathematics is communicated. Seeing the general in the particular, recognizing patterns and relationships of dependence between variables and expressing them through different representations, as well as the modeling of mathematical situations or the real world with symbolic expressions, are fundamental characteristics of the algebraic sense, but they are also characteristics of computational thinking, which serves to formulate, represent and solve problems through tools and concepts specific to computer science.

The stochastic sense includes the analysis and interpretation of data, the elaboration of conjectures and decision-making based on statistical information, its critical assessment and the understanding and communication of random phenomena in a wide variety of everyday situations.

The socio-emotional sense integrates knowledge, skills and attitudes to understand and manage emotions, set and achieve goals, increase the ability to make responsible and informed decisions, which is aimed at improving student performance in mathematics, reducing negative attitudes towards mathematics, promoting active learning and eradicating preconceived ideas related to gender or the myth of indispensable innate talent. To reinforce this purpose, it is essential to make students aware of the contributions of women to mathematics throughout history and in the present day. Knowledge corresponding to this point must be explicitly included throughout the development of the entire curriculum.

Both the specific skills, the assessment criteria and the knowledge are designed to constitute a whole that facilitates the approach to complex tasks, individual or collective, in different, meaningful and relevant contexts that allow the fundamental aspects of mathematics to be developed.

In the Mathematics subject, a total of 9 specific skills are worked on, which are the concretization of the operational indicators of the key skills defined in the students' exit skill profile at the end of basic education.

**Specific competence 1**

**Interpret, model and solve everyday life situations, specific to mathematics and other areas of knowledge, applying different strategies and forms of reasoning to explore procedures and obtain solutions.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 1.1 Interpret mathematical problems by organizing the information given and understanding the questions asked.  1.2 Develop effective mathematical representations, with manipulable, graphic and digital resources, that lead to the understanding and resolution of problems and situations in everyday life.  1.3 Analyze and select tools and strategies developed by evaluating and contrasting their effectiveness and suitability in a reasoned way in solving problems.  1.4 Obtain mathematical solutions to a problem by mobilizing the necessary knowledge and discriminating the existence or not of one or more solutions to a problem. | 1.1 Interpret mathematical problems by organizing the information given and understanding the questions asked.  1.2 Develop effective mathematical representations, with manipulable, graphic and digital resources, that lead to the understanding and resolution of problems and situations in everyday life.  1.3 Analyze and select tools and strategies developed by evaluating and contrasting their effectiveness and suitability in a reasoned way in solving problems.  1.4 Obtain mathematical solutions to a problem by mobilizing the necessary knowledge and discriminating the existence or not of one or more solutions to a problem. |

Problem solving is a fundamental axis in learning mathematics, as it is a central process in the construction of mathematical knowledge. Both the situations of everyday life in different contexts and the problems proposed in the field of mathematics can be catalysts for new knowledge, since the reflections that are carried out during their resolution help to build concepts and establish connections between them.

The development of this competence involves applying the mathematical knowledge that students have in the context of problem solving. For this, it is necessary to provide interpretation and modeling tools such as diagrams, symbolic expressions, graphics..., problem-solving techniques and strategies such as analogy with other problems, estimation, trial and error, solving it in reverse, from the end to the beginning, estimation, decomposition into simpler problems..., which allow them to make decisions, anticipate the answer, take risks and accept the error as part of the process.

**Specific competence 2**

**Arguing the suitability of solutions to a problem, evaluating the answers obtained through reasoning and mathematical logic, to verify their validity and generate new questions and challenges.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 2.1 Construct and coherently express ideas and reasoning that allow to justify the validity of solutions, processes and conclusions from different perspectives (gender, sustainability, responsible consumption...).  2.2 Generate questions based on mathematical arguments that allow us to raise new challenges related to the solved problem. | 2.1 Construct and coherently express ideas and reasoning that allow to justify the validity of solutions, processes and conclusions from different perspectives (gender, sustainability, responsible consumption...).  2.2 Generate questions based on mathematical arguments that allow us to raise new challenges related to the solved problem |

The analysis of the solutions obtained in the resolution of a problem enhances critical reflection on its validity, both from a strictly mathematical point of view and from a global perspective, valuing aspects related to sustainability, responsible consumption, equity or non-discrimination among others. Scientific and mathematical reasoning are the main tools to carry out this validation, but so are careful reading, asking appropriate questions, choosing strategies to verify the relevance of the solutions obtained according to the situation at hand, awareness of one's own progress and self-evaluation.

The development of this competence involves reflective processes specific to metacognition such as the act and co-evaluation, the use of simple self-regulated learning strategies, effective use of digital tools such as calculators or spreadsheets, the verbalization or explanation of the process and the selection between different methods of checking solutions or strategies to validate the solutions and their scope.

**Specific competence 3**

**Formulate simple conjectures or problems, using reasoning and argumentation, creativity and technological tools, to integrate and generate new mathematical knowledge.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 3.1 Ask questions in various contexts that can be answered through mathematical knowledge.  3.2 Make simple mathematical conjectures autonomously and reasoned in a context in which the student has creative freedom making use, if necessary, of technological tools (programming languages, spreadsheets, GeoGebra, mathematical photography, video, etc.).  3.3 Propose problems autonomously, creatively and reasoned in a context. | 3.1 Ask questions in various contexts that can be answered through mathematical knowledge.  3.2 Make simple mathematical conjectures autonomously and reasoned in a context in which the student has creative freedom making use, if necessary, of technological tools (programming languages, spreadsheets, GeoGebra, mathematical photography, video, etc.).  3.3 Propose problems autonomously, creatively and reasoned in a context. |

Reasoning and analytical thinking increase the perception of patterns, structures and regularities in both real-world and abstract situations by favoring the formulation of conjectures about their nature. The formulation and verification of conjectures can be carried out by means of manipulative materials, calculators, software, representations and symbols, working individually or collectively using inductive and deductive reasoning to formulate mathematical arguments.

The development of this competence involves formulating conjectures, examining their validity and reformulating them to obtain new conjectures that can be tested by promoting the use of reasoning and demonstration as fundamental aspects of mathematics.

**Specific competence 4**

**Use computational thinking, organizing data, decomposing it into parts, pattern recognition, interpreting, modifying, generalizing and creating algorithms** **to model situations and solve problems efficiently.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 4.1 Break down a problem or situation in everyday life into different parts, tackling them one at a time to be able to find the global solution with digital devices.  4.2 Recognize patterns, similarities and trends in the problems or situations to be solved.  4.3 Find the principles that generate the patterns of a problem by discarding irrelevant data while identifying the most important parts.  4.4 Generate step-by-step instructions to solve a problem and similar ones by testing and carrying out possible solutions with digital devices. | 4.1 Break down a problem or situation in everyday life into different parts, tackling them one at a time to be able to find the global solution with digital devices.  4.2 Recognize patterns, similarities and trends in the problems or situations to be solved.  4.3 Find the principles that generate the patterns of a problem by discarding irrelevant data while identifying the most important parts.  4.4 Generate step-by-step instructions to solve a problem and similar ones by testing and carrying out possible solutions with digital devices. |

Computational thinking is directly related to the resolution of challenges or problems and the formulation of procedures, using abstraction to identify the most relevant aspects, and the decomposition into simpler tasks with the aim of reaching a solution to the problem that can be executed by a computer system. Bringing computational thinking into daily life means relating the fundamental aspects of computer science to the needs of students.

The development of this competence entails the creation of abstract models of everyday situations, their automation and modeling and the coding in a language that is easy to interpret by a computer system.

**Specific competence 5**

**Connect different mathematical elements** **relating concepts, procedures, arguments and models to develop a view of mathematics as an integrated whole.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 5.1 Identify and use the connections between different representations of the same mathematical concept when information is extracted from one of them to apply it to the other.  5.2 Recognize and relate connections between different concepts and mathematical knowledge through everyday life situations to draw conclusions and have an integrated vision of mathematics. | 5.1 Identify and use the connections between different representations of the same mathematical concept when information is extracted from one of them to apply it to the other.  5.2 Recognize and relate connections between different concepts and mathematical knowledge through everyday life situations to draw conclusions and have an integrated vision of mathematics. |

The connection between the different mathematical concepts, procedures and ideas brings a deeper and lasting understanding of the acquired knowledge, providing a broader view about the knowledge itself. Perceiving mathematics as a whole involves studying its internal connections and reflecting on these, both those existing between blocks of knowledge, between the mathematics of one level and those of different educational stages.

The development of this competence involves linking new mathematical ideas with previous ideas, recognizing and using the connections between mathematical ideas in problem solving, and understanding how some ideas build on others to form an integrated whole.

**Specific competence 6**

**Linking and contextualizing mathematics with other areas of knowledge**, **interrelating concepts and procedures**, **to solve problems and develop critical, creative and innovative capacity in various situations.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 6.1 Recognize and use the mathematics present in everyday life using the processes inherent in scientific and mathematical research: infer, measure, communicate, classify, predict..., in situations likely to be addressed in mathematical terms.  6.2 Recognize and use the connections between mathematics and other subjects, in situations that can be addressed in mathematical terms.  6.3 Identify and value the current and historical contribution of mathematics to the progress of humanity, also from a gender perspective, in the face of the challenges posed by today's society.  6.4 Develop the critical spirit and creative potential of mathematics by arguing innovative proposals in scientific, technological, social, artistic and cultural contexts. | 6.1 Recognize and use the mathematics present in everyday life using the processes inherent in scientific and mathematical research: infer, measure, communicate, classify, predict..., in situations likely to be addressed in mathematical terms.  6.2 Recognize and use the connections between mathematics and other subjects, in situations that can be addressed in mathematical terms.  6.3 Identify and value the current and historical contribution of mathematics to the progress of humanity, also from a gender perspective, in the face of the challenges posed by today's society.  6.4 Develop the critical spirit and creative potential of mathematics by arguing innovative proposals in scientific, technological, social, artistic and cultural contexts. |

Recognizing and using the connection of mathematics with other subjects, with real life or with one's own experience increases the students' mathematical background. It is important that students have the opportunity to experience mathematics in different contexts (personal, school, social, scientific and humanistic), valuing, both historically and currently, the contribution of mathematics to the resolution of the major global development goals.

The connection between mathematics and other subjects should not be limited to conceptual knowledge, but should be extended to procedures and attitudes, so that mathematical procedures and attitudes can be transferred and applied to other subjects and contexts. Thus, the development of this competence entails the establishment of connections between ideas, concepts and mathematical procedures with other subjects and with real life and their application in solving problems in various situations and developing critical, creative and innovative capacity in various situations.

**Specific competence 7**

**Communicate and represent, individually and collectively, mathematical concepts, procedures and results using oral, written, graphic, multimodal language and the appropriate mathematical terminology, to give meaning and permanence to mathematical ideas.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 7.1 Communicate information in an organized manner, using appropriate mathematical language, orally and in writing, to describe, explain and justify reasoning, procedures and conclusions.  7.2 Represent mathematical concepts, procedures and results clearly, using different tools and forms of expression, such as through drawing, photography, videos, visual and musical works, to visualize ideas and structure mathematical processes.  7.3 Dialogue with peers and debate mathematical ideas to describe, explain and justify reasoning, processes and conclusions. | 7.1 Communicate information in an organized manner, using appropriate mathematical language, orally and in writing, to describe, explain and justify reasoning, procedures and conclusions.  7.2 Represent mathematical concepts, procedures and results clearly, using different tools and forms of expression, such as through drawing, photography, videos, visual and musical works, to visualize ideas and structure mathematical processes.  7.3 Dialogue with peers and debate mathematical ideas to describe, explain and justify reasoning, processes and conclusions. |

Communication and the exchange of ideas is an essential part of science and mathematics education. Through communication ideas become objects of reflection, refinement, discussion and rectification. Communicating ideas, concepts and processes contributes to collaborating, cooperating, strengthening and generating new knowledge.

The development of this competence entails expressing facts, ideas, concepts and procedures verbally and graphically, truthfully and precisely using the appropriate mathematical terminology, giving meaning and permanence to the ideas and making them public.

The use of oral, written, graphic, multimodal language entails the development of skills in the use of different languages ​​and tools, in particular digital ones. The way ideas, concepts and procedures are represented in mathematics is fundamental. The representation includes two facets, the actual representation of a result or concept and the representation of the processes that are carried out during the practice of mathematics.

The development of this competence entails the acquisition of a set of mathematical representations that significantly expands the ability to interpret and solve real-life problems.

**Specific competence 8**

**Develop personal skills, such as self-regulation, that help identify and manage emotions, learning from mistakes and facing situations of uncertainty as an opportunity, to persevere and enjoy the process of learning mathematics.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 8.1 Manage one's emotions and develop self-confidence to face new mathematical challenges by persevering in solving them in any proposed learning situation.  8.2 Be aware that you are learning and how you are learning in any proposed learning situation 8.3 Identify your own mistakes and express in a reasoned way what is the reason that causes them (conceptual, procedural, strategy...), in the resolution of challenges or problems, persevering in their resolution.  8.4 Participate in the evaluation itself by managing strategies that help overcome difficulties, in the review of the productions carried out.   8.5 Appreciate the creative potential of mathematics as well as its ability to generate harmony and beauty, in the creations and productions carried out. | 8.1 Manage one's emotions and develop self-confidence to face new mathematical challenges by persevering in solving them in any proposed learning situation.  8.2 Be aware that you are learning and how you are learning in any proposed learning situation 8.3 Identify your own mistakes and express in a reasoned way what is the reason that causes them (conceptual, procedural, strategy...), in the resolution of challenges or problems, persevering in their resolution.  8.4 Participate in the evaluation itself by managing strategies that help overcome difficulties, in the review of the productions carried out.   8.5 Appreciate the creative potential of mathematics as well as its ability to generate harmony and beauty, in the creations and productions carried out. |

Solving mathematical problems or more global challenges involving mathematics should be a rewarding task. Emotional skills in learning mathematics promote students' well-being, emotional regulation and interest in their learning.

The development of this competence involves identifying and managing emotions, recognizing sources of stress, persevering, thinking critically and creatively, building resilience and maintaining a proactive attitude towards new mathematical challenges.

**Specific competence 9**

**Develop social skills, such as cooperation, actively participating in inclusive work teams recognizing the diversity and value of others' contributions, to share and build mathematical knowledge collectively.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st, 2nd and 3rd | 4th |
| --- | --- | 
| 9.1 Cooperate in teamwork both in face-to-face and virtual environments, listening to others and valuing their contributions, respecting the gender perspective, in situations where knowledge is shared and built together.  9.2 Collaborate actively with others, reaching agreements and complying with them, to achieve the group's objectives related to the construction of mathematical knowledge, valuing collective success as a strategy for personal improvement.  9.3. Balance personal needs with those of the group, based on empathy and respect, recognizing the diversity and value of the contributions of others to generate new mathematical learning, both individual and collective.  9.4. Help identify mistakes and learning difficulties of colleagues by making constructive and concrete contributions that can help overcome them and improve. | 9.1 Cooperate in teamwork both in face-to-face and virtual environments, listening to others and valuing their contributions, respecting the gender perspective, in situations where knowledge is shared and built together.  9.2 Collaborate actively with others, reaching agreements and complying with them, to achieve the group's objectives related to the construction of mathematical knowledge, valuing collective success as a strategy for personal improvement.  9.3. Balance personal needs with those of the group, based on empathy and respect, recognizing the diversity and value of the contributions of others to generate new mathematical learning, both individual and collective.  9.4. Help identify mistakes and learning difficulties of colleagues by making constructive and concrete contributions that can help overcome them and improve. |

The development of this competence involves showing empathy for others, establishing and maintaining positive relationships, exercising active listening and assertive communication, working in a team and making responsible decisions. Likewise, the breakdown of stereotypes and preconceived ideas about mathematics associated with individual issues, such as gender or aptitude for mathematics, must be encouraged.

Working on the values ​​of respect, tolerance, equality or peaceful resolution of conflicts, at the same time as they solve mathematical challenges by developing effective communication skills, planning, inquiry, motivation, trust, to create healthy relationships and work environments, allows to strengthen self-confidence and normalize situations of coexistence in equality.

Virtual environments are a good tool for sharing and building knowledge together, in this sense it is necessary to promote their use.

**Knows**

Knowledge, understood as the set of knowledge, skills, values ​​and attitudes, are formulated in relation to contexts where their learning skills can be developed. Teachers can incorporate alternative contexts if they consider it relevant.

In order to facilitate learning and the development of the corresponding specific skills, teachers can assess the possibility of organizing the knowledge of the subject, or of the different subjects coordinated in an area, based on situations.

The situations make it possible to program the course of any level, subject or area from a collection or sequence of challenges, contexts, circumstances of the real world, from which derive questions that need to be answered and that intertwine knowledge, that is, knowledge, skills, values ​​and attitudes with the capacities that support the competence approach to learning. This modifies the usual planning for the acquisition of knowledge and skills based on the academic logic specific to the areas of knowledge or subjects, embodied in the traditional sequence of disciplinary subjects. It aims to approach the learner's logic to give meaning to their learning based on the sequence of relevant contexts embodied in the situations.

**From first to third year**

**Number Sense**

- counting
	- Solving problems and situations in everyday life in which systematic counting must be done, using different strategies (tree diagrams, combinatorics techniques, etc.).
- quantity
	- Interpretation of large and small numbers, recognition and use of exponential and scientific notation. Including the reading of these amounts in the calculator or spreadsheet
	- Expression of estimates with the required precision.
	- Use of whole numbers, fractions, decimals and roots to express quantities in different contexts, including those of everyday life, with the required precision.
	- Use of Indo-Arabic numbers, the introduction of zero and negative numbers in the history of mathematics.
	- Use of fractions in antiquity (Egypt, India and Greece) and today.
	- Recognition and application of different forms of representation of whole numbers, fractions and decimals, including the number line.
	- Selection and use of the most appropriate representation of the same quantity (natural, whole, decimal or fraction) for each situation or problem.
- Sense of operations
	- Application of mental calculation strategies with natural numbers, fractions and decimals.
	- Recognition and application of operations with whole numbers, fractions or decimals useful for solving contextualized situations.
	- Understanding and using inverse relationships, between: addition and subtraction, multiplication and division, powers and roots, to simplify and solve problems.
	- Interpretation of the effects of arithmetic operations with whole numbers, fractions and decimal expressions.
	- Using the properties of arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication and division) to perform calculations efficiently with natural numbers, integers, fractions and decimals both mentally and manually, with a calculator or spreadsheet, adapting strategies to each situation.
- relationships
	- Using prime factors, multiples and divisors to solve problems, using various strategies and/or tools, including the use of the calculator.
	- Comparing and ordering fractions, decimals and percentages effectively by finding their exact or approximate position on the number line.
- Proportional reasoning
	- Identification of proportional and non-proportional situations (including inverse proportionality situations) in everyday life problems. Understanding and representation of quantitative relationships.
	- Percentages: understanding and use in problem solving, including those greater than 100% or less than 1%.
	- Development and analysis of methods to solve problems in situations of direct proportionality in different contexts (percentage increases and decreases, price reductions and increases, taxes, currency changes, geometric calculations, scales, etc.).
- Financial education
	- Interpretation of numerical information in simple financial contexts.
	- Methods for making responsible consumption decisions given the quality-price and value-price relationships in everyday contexts.

**Sense of measurement**

- Magnitude
	- Measurable attributes of physical and mathematical objects: research and relationship between them.
	- Choice of appropriate units and operations in situations involving measurement.
	- Comparison of the units of the decimal metric system with others present in different contexts.
	- Evaluation of the importance of the establishment of the meter as a universal measure in the historical context in which it was produced and in the current context.
- measurement
	- Selection and use of instruments (analogue or digital) and suitable units to directly measure different magnitudes of the environment.
	- Deduction, interpretation and application of the main strategies to obtain lengths, areas and volumes in flat and three-dimensional figures.
	- Relationship between the applications of the theorems of Thales and Pythagoras in the different historical contexts in which they have been used (Greece, India, China).
	- Use of flat representations of three-dimensional objects to visualize and solve area problems, among others.
	- Generation of flat representations, manually or digitally, of flat or three-dimensional geometric objects, with given characteristics, such as side lengths, angle measurements, edge lengths.
- Estimation and relationships
	- Formulation of conjectures about measurements or relationships between them based on estimates.
	- Justified decision making of the degree of precision required in measurement situations.
	- Evaluation of measurements of the radius of the Earth and of the Earth-Moon distances in ancient Greece.

**Spatial Sense**

- Geometric shapes of two and three dimensions
	- Description and classification of flat and three-dimensional geometric shapes based on their properties or characteristics.
	- Recognition of geometric relationships such as congruence, similarity and the Pythagorean relationship in flat and three-dimensional figures.
	- Construction of geometric shapes with different tools: manipulable materials, drawing tools, dynamic geometry programs, augmented reality, etc.
	- Construction of geometric figures in different historical contexts, in particular in ancient Greece (Euclid).
- Location and representation systems
	- Location and description of spatial relationships: geometric coordinates and other systems of representation.
- Movements and transformations
	- Analyzes of elementary transformations such as rotations, translations and symmetries in various situations using technological and/or manipulative tools.
- Visualization and geometric modeling
	- Use of geometric models to represent and explain numerical and algebraic relationships in various situations.
	- Recognition of connections between the spatial sense with the other senses (numerical, algebraic...) and with other disciplines (art, science, daily life).

**Algebraic Sense**

- patterns
	- Patterns: identification and understanding, determining the rule of formation of numerical or graphic collections.
	- Formulas and general terms: obtained through the observation of simple guidelines and regularities and their generalization.
	- Identification of the Fibonacci sequence and the golden ratio in nature.
- Mathematical model
	- Modeling and solving contextualized problems, also from everyday life, supported by mathematical representations and algebraic language.
	- Obtaining reasonable conclusions about a daily life situation once modeled.
- variable
	- Understanding the concept of variable in its different natures.
- Equality and inequality
	- Use of symbolic algebra to represent linear and quadratic relationships in contextualized situations, also from everyday life.
	- Analysis of the different methods of solving equations throughout history, in particular the geometric methods of Al-Khwarizmi.
	- Identification and application of the equivalence of algebraic expressions in solving problems based on linear and quadratic relationships.
	- Search for solutions in equations or linear systems and quadratic equations, both manually and using technology.
- Relations and functions
	- Application and comparison of the different forms of representation of a relationship.
	- Identification and use of linear or non-linear functions and comparison of their properties from tables, graphs or algebraic expressions.
	- Identification of quantitative relationships in contextualized situations, including everyday life and determination of the types of functions that model them (linear and quadratic).
	- Deduction of relevant information from a function through the use of different symbolic representations.
- Computational thinking
	- Identification and use of strategies when interpreting, modifying or creating block programming algorithms and/or textual programming that incorporate: differentiation between sequential and parallel processes; understanding loop statements, conditionals, and nested statements; understanding of data management with variables; use of logical operators and events.
	- Formulation of issues capable of being analyzed using programs and other tools.

**Sense Stochastic**

- distribution
	- Analysis and interpretation of statistical tables and graphs of qualitative, discrete quantitative and continuous quantitative variables.
	- Collection and organization of data from contextualized situations, including everyday life, involving a single variable.
	- Generation of appropriate graphic representations using different technologies (calculator, spreadsheet, apps...) to find out how the data is distributed, interpret it and obtain reasoned conclusions.
	- Measures of centralization and dispersion: interpretation and calculation.
	- Comparison of two sets of data given the measures of centralization and dispersion.
	- Recognition that measures of dispersion describe the variability of data.
	- Calculation, with technological support, and interpretation of centralization and dispersion measures in real situations.
- inference
	- Formulation of appropriate questions to find out the characteristics of interest of a population.
	- Presentation of relevant data to answer questions raised in statistical research.
	- Obtaining reasonable conclusions from the results obtained in order to issue judgments and make appropriate decisions.
	- Use of statistical data throughout history in the construction of population censuses.
	- Uses of statistical data in current medicine (covid 19) and in history, the case of Florence Nightingale.
- Predictability and uncertainty
	- Identification of deterministic and random phenomena.
	- Interpretation of probability as a measure associated with the uncertainty of random experiments.
	- Planning and carrying out simple experiments to analyze the behavior of random phenomena.
	- Assignment of probability based on experimentation and the concept of relative frequency.
	- Analysis of the origin of the theory of probability (Fermat and Pascal) in the context of gambling.
	- Assigning probabilities using Laplace's rule.

**Socio-emotional sense**

- Beliefs, attitudes and emotions
	- Development of curiosity, initiative, perseverance and resilience towards learning mathematics.
	- Management of the emotions involved in learning such as self-awareness and self-regulation.
	- Development of the cognitive flexibility to accept a change of strategy when necessary and transform the error into a learning opportunity and in turn, interpret each solved problem as an opportunity to generate new questions.
- Teamwork and decision making
	- Assumption of responsibilities and active participation to optimize teamwork.
	- Selection of cooperative techniques to share and build knowledge collectively.
	- Use of management strategies and appropriate decision-making to resolve situations specific to teamwork.

**Fourth year**

Given that this subject is taught in compulsory secondary education, it has been chosen not to differentiate between Mathematics A (more general) and Mathematics B (more academic). More academic knowledge that is not considered basic for everyone has been marked with (\*).

**Number Sense**

- counting
	- Solving problems and situations in everyday life in which systematic counting must be done, using different strategies (tree diagrams, combinatorics techniques, etc.).
- quantity
	- Expression of estimates in various contexts analyzing the error committed.
	- Use of real numbers to express quantities in different contexts, including everyday life, with the required accuracy
	- Recognition and application of different forms of representation of whole, rational and real numbers, including the number line, suitable for each situation or problem.
	- Identification of the numerical set that serves to respond to different needs: count, measure, compare, etc.
- Sense of operations
	- Choosing the right operations with real numbers to solve contextualized situations.
	- Using the properties of arithmetic operations to perform calculations with real numbers efficiently with a calculator and sometimes by hand, adapting strategies to each situation.
	- Recognition of some irrational numbers in everyday situations.
	- Historical evolution of the different approximations to the number pi.
	- Identification and analysis of numerical patterns and regularities involving real numbers.

- relationships
	- Comparing and ordering real numbers effectively by finding their exact or approximate location on the number line.
	- Use of the arithmetic triangle throughout history to solve problems.
- Financial education
	- Development, analysis and explanation of methods for solving problems related to percentage increases and decreases, interest and rates in financial contexts.

**Sense of measurement**

- measurement
	- Deduction of the measures of the elements of a triangle in situations that can be modeled with right triangles.
	- (\*) Use of trigonometric ratios and their relationships in solving problems that can be modeled with right triangles.
	- Origin and use of trigonometry throughout history and in particular to measure the Earth-Sun and Earth-Moon distance.

**Spatial Sense**

- Geometric shapes of two and three dimensions
	- Elaboration of conjectures and recognition of geometric properties of flat and three-dimensional figures through research with dynamic geometry programs.
	- Use of geometric properties of flat and three-dimensional figures that model everyday life situations.
	- Location and representation systems.
	- Use of basic notions of analytical geometry for the representation of two-dimensional geometric figures and the analysis of their properties.
	- Origin and historical evolution of the use of Cartesian coordinates.
	- (\*) Recognition of different algebraic expressions of a straight line and selection of the most appropriate expression depending on the situation to be solved.
- Movements and transformations
	- Analysis of elementary transformations including homothecies in various situations using technological and/or manipulative tools (\*) or through the use of analytical geometry.
- Visualization and geometric modeling
	- Generation of geometric models to represent and explain numerical and algebraic relationships in various situations, including everyday ones.

**Algebraic sense**

- patterns
	- Understanding and analyzing patterns, determining the rule of formation of various numerical or graphic collections.
- Mathematical model
	- Modeling and solving contextualized problems, also from everyday life, using mathematical representations and algebraic language, making use of different types of functions.
	- Obtaining and analyzing reasonable conclusions from a daily life situation once modeled.
- variable
	- Use of the different uses of variables by associating symbolic expressions with the context of the problem.
	- Historical evolution of the variable concept and the use of symbolic algebra as a language of science.
- Equality and inequality
	- Use of symbolic algebra to represent functional relationships in various contexts, including everyday life.
	- Use and generation of equivalent forms of algebraic expressions in solving linear inequalities.
- Relations and functions
	- Identification and use of the most appropriate form of representation of elementary functions in the resolution of contextualized situations, including everyday life
	- Identification of quantitative relationships in contextualized situations, including everyday life and determination of the types of functions that model them (inverse proportionality and exponential)
	- Interpretation of different characteristics of change through the graphical representation of the studied functional relationships.
- Computational thinking
	- Identification and analysis of strategies (sequences of ordered steps, schemes, simulations, repetitive patterns, loops, nested and conditional instructions, computational representations, block programming, educational robotics...) for the interpretation, modification and creation of algorithms.
	- Identification and analysis of strategies when interpreting, modifying or creating block programming algorithms and/or textual programming that incorporate: differentiation between sequential and parallel processes; understanding loop statements, conditionals, and nested statements; understanding of data management with variables; use of logical operators and events.
	- Formulation and analysis of everyday life problems using appropriate programs and tools.

**Sense Stochastic**

- distribution
	- Analysis and interpretation of statistical tables and graphs of two qualitative variables, discrete quantitative and continuous quantitative.
	- Collection and organization of data from contextualized situations, including everyday life that involve two variables.
	- Generation of graphic representations through the use of appropriate technological means to interpret statistical information and obtain reasoned conclusions.
	- Comparison of data distributions taking into account measures of position and dispersion.
- inference
	- Design of statistical studies reflecting on the different stages of the statistical process.
	- Presentation and interpretation of relevant data in statistical research through the use of statistical methods and appropriate digital tools.
	- Interpretation of the relationship between two variables, assessing graphically with technological tools the relevance of a linear regression.
	- Historical evolution of the application of statistics to the social sciences.
- Predictability and uncertainty
	- Planning and carrying out simple and compound experiments to study the behavior of random phenomena.
	- Application of the calculation of probabilities to make informed decisions in different contexts, applying Laplace's rule and counting techniques in simple and compound experiments.

**Socio-emotional sense**

- Beliefs, attitudes and emotions
	- Development of curiosity, initiative, perseverance and resilience towards learning mathematics.
	- Management of the emotions involved in learning such as self-awareness and self-regulation.
	- Development of the cognitive flexibility to accept a change of strategy when necessary and transform the error into a learning opportunity and in turn, interpret each solved problem as an opportunity to generate new questions.
- Teamwork and decision making
	- Assumption of responsibilities and active participation to optimize teamwork.
	- Selection of cooperative techniques to share and build knowledge collectively.
	- Use of management strategies and appropriate decision-making to resolve situations specific to teamwork
</div>
</div>
</div>

<div class="accordion-item">
<h2 class="accordion-header" id="headingRob">
<button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#collapseRob" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="collapseRob">
<strong>🤖 Robotics and programming</strong>
</button>
</h2>
<div id="collapseRob" class="accordion-collapse collapse" aria-labelledby="headingRob" data-bs-parent="#competenciasAccordion">
<div class="accordion-body">

**[Robotics and Programming](https://xtec.gencat.cat/web/.content/curriculum/eso/curriculum-175-2022/Robotica-i-Programacio.pdf "Robotica and Programming"){target="_blank"}**

This optional subject aims for students to develop skills to come up with innovative and creative solutions in solving problems through the design, programming and prototyping of automated systems and robots

The skills must be worked on in the context of learning situations, connected to reality and which invite students to reflection, collaboration and action.

The achievement of the specific skills constitutes the basis for the student's competence assessment and will be assessed through the assessment criteria. There is no unequivocal and direct link between assessment criteria and knowledge, specific skills will be assessed through the implementation of different knowledge, providing the necessary flexibility to establish connections between them.

Approaching a competence approach, the evaluation criteria and knowledge are structured around specific competences. This progression, which starts from very close and manipulative environments connecting with the stages of infant and primary education, facilitates the transition towards more formal learning and favors the development of the ability to think abstractly.

The assessment criteria, as they explain the assessment of the skills and knowledge that needs to be developed, specify the learning we want to identify in the students and the way to do it. They are directly linked to specific skills. The evaluation criteria make it possible to measure the degree of development of these skills and the teacher can flexibly connect them with the knowledge of the area or the subject during the teaching-learning process.

The teaching staff must contextualize and make these criteria more flexible in accordance with the circumstances of their activity. Their character is markedly competitive and makes them evaluators of both the capabilities deployed and the different types of knowledge, that is, knowledge, skills, values ​​and attitudes that students must acquire in order to develop in multiple situations typical of modern society.

The use of *computational thinking and design thinking* strategies is considered very useful for the achievement of capacities that help develop solutions and prototypes that respond to specific needs, incorporating strategies for analysis, ideation, creation and evaluation of solutions.

The most suitable work methodology for the subject is the integration of all these concepts in a project, enabling teamwork and using collaborative project management and organization techniques. However, the orientation of the subject must enable the development of the necessary skills in the use of different digital programming, design and construction tools.

This subject contributes to the achievement of learning that is adaptable for life and to fostering vocations within the scientific, technological and mathematical fields, giving students the opportunity to identify real-world problems and find realistic solutions, encouraging creativity, curiosity, personalized analysis, the exchange of ideas and cooperative work.

The active involvement of students in the creation of quality designed solutions for the needs and opportunities identified in various technological contexts encourages their personal development. Students manage projects autonomously and collaboratively from conception to completion. They apply design processes to research, generate and refine ideas, plan, produce and evaluate designed solutions and improve their ability to develop innovative products and environments.

The knowledge of the subject is organized in three blocks.

The first block, *design thinking strategies and collaborative project management*, covers project development by applying design processes to research, generate and refine ideas, plan, produce and evaluate designed solutions and develop their capacity to develop innovative products and environments.

The second block, *computational thinking, programming languages ​​and structures* aims to understand the fundamentals of algorithms for the design and development of programs, and the application of specific techniques such as the creation of flow diagrams or the decomposition of complex problems into simple ones.

The third block, *design and construction of robots* allows the production of the elements and structures necessary for the functioning of the prototypes, as well as the interaction with the environment through the collection of data with sensors and the action through actuators.

In the field of Robotics and Programming, a total of 4 specific skills are worked on, which are the realization of the operational indicators of the key skills defined in the students' exit skill profile at the end of basic education.

**Specific competence 1**

**Design creative and functional prototypes to respond to specific problems and challenges from collaborative projects, using design thinking techniques.**

**Evaluation criteria**

1.1 Identify and analyze specific problems or challenges, break them down into simpler parts that allow their solution.

1.2 Collaboratively define and evaluate the possible solutions to the problems and challenges analyzed, assessing their viability and sustainability.

1.3 Argue and share ideas in a group to solve a common problem, with a respectful attitude.

1.4 Plan designs, taking into account the functionalities to be developed, with an entrepreneurial and creative attitude, integrating the appropriate mechanical and electronic elements.

1.5 Use different tools and supports for the design of the prototype and for its prior assessment.

This specific competence addresses all phases of any technical project: defining the problem or need to be solved, researching from multiple sources, devising different solutions, designing and evaluating them. The aim is to apply all the phases of the process in a real project, and do it iteratively until the most suitable design is achieved.

**Specific competence 2**

**Apply computational thinking strategies in an organized and optimal way to create, rework or improve algorithms that help solve real problems.**

**Evaluation criteria**

2.1 Analyze processes using logical thinking strategies.

2.2 Describe and represent logical sequences that help to understand processes or algorithms using flow diagrams.

2.3 Develop programs that involve sequencing of steps, iteration, and testing, validation, and debugging of sequences.

2.4 Compare own programs with other algorithms that solve the same problem, incorporating the necessary changes or combining different programs to develop new solutions.

This competence encompasses the knowledge of specific techniques and strategies of computational thinking, understood as a process that generates open solutions. It includes the decomposition of complex problems into simple ones, and representation of processes in logical sequences, as well as elements of logic and human thought such as generalization.

These strategies must allow the generation of a finite set of instructions or steps that must be used to generate algorithms that provide solutions to real problems. However, the comparison between own programs with other algorithms, and the combination of different programs to develop new solutions must be part of this solution generation process.

**Specific competence 3**

**Configure and program programmable prototyping boards and sensors and actuators that allow responding to challenges or problems, using logical structures from programming languages.**

**Evaluation criteria**

3.1 Develop programs, or rework them from existing programs, using software and programming languages ​​appropriately.

3.2 Use logical structures appropriately, taking into account program optimization criteria.

3.3 Identify, correct and debug programming errors in computer programs, using debuggers.

3.4 Configure and program sensors and actuators, adjusting them to the needs of the prototype and making correct use of their functionalities.

The competence refers to the development of programs in different programming languages, making use of logical structures, functions, variables and all the necessary elements for the development of organized and optimized algorithms.

The competence covers the knowledge of the functionalities of the different sensors and actuators that enable interaction with the physical world, through the acquisition of data and the automation of movements.

**Specific competence 4**

**Build structures and mechanisms to respond to the necessary mechanical requirements, from specific components or designed and produced through the use of digital design tools.**

**Evaluation criteria**

4.1 Design, using digital tools and suitable software, the elements necessary for the physical construction of the designed prototypes, the assembly of sensors, actuators and mechanical systems.

4.2 Produce or manufacture the necessary elements for the implementation of structures and mechanisms, safely using the appropriate tools, devices, techniques and materials.

4.3 Carry out the physical assembly of structures and mechanisms, and evaluate the design and construction.

This competence refers, on the one hand, to the digital or manual design of elements and structures, and on the other to manual construction processes and mechanical manufacturing or digital printing. It involves the application of knowledge related to operators and technological systems (structural, mechanical, electrical and electronic) necessary to build or manufacture prototypes based on prior design and planning.

Likewise, the application of safety rules when working with materials, tools and machines are fundamental for the health of students, avoiding the risks inherent in many of the techniques that must be used.

**Knows**

The knowledge is formulated in relation to contexts where their learning skills can be developed. Teachers can incorporate alternative contexts if they consider it relevant.

In order to facilitate learning and the development of the corresponding specific skills, teachers can assess the possibility of organizing the knowledge of the subject, or of the different subjects coordinated in an area, based on situations.

The situations make it possible to program the course of any level, subject or area from a collection or sequence of challenges, contexts, circumstances of the real world, from which derive questions that need to be answered and that intertwine knowledge, that is, knowledge, skills, values ​​and attitudes with the capacities that support the competence approach to learning. This modifies the usual planning for the acquisition of knowledge and skills based on the academic logic specific to the areas of knowledge or subjects, embodied in the traditional sequence of disciplinary subjects. It aims to approach the learner's logic to give meaning to their learning based on the sequence of relevant contexts embodied in the situations.

**A. Design thinking strategies and collaborative project management**

- Design of solutions to problems raised in accordance with design thinking.
- Application of basic project management strategies: definition of objectives, planning, project execution and evaluation.

**B. Computational thinking, programming languages ​​and structures**

- Application of computational thinking techniques in solving problems and designing solutions.
- Analysis and decomposition of complex problems into simple challenges. Efficient resolution strategies.
- Representation of solutions using flow diagrams, taking into account specific regulations.
- Use of programming languages ​​with application of different logical structures: sequences, conditionals and repetitions.
- Development of specific functions.

**C. Robot design and construction**

- Analysis of mechanical elements and identification of their operation.
- Configuration and programming of the different control elements: sensors, actuators and control devices.
- Design and construction of simple elements and/or structures, both in real form and through graphic simulators, 3D and 2D design programs.
- Physical assembly of structures and mechanisms, making appropriate use of tools and applying safety measures.
- Application of manual creation techniques and digital manufacturing.
- Critical assessment of technological advances, their influence on the environment, individual and collective health and well-being and society in general.
